title: Major Italian bank defrauded of millions via AI deception
content:
MILAN (ANP/RTR) – Scammers used AI tools to steal €95 million from the private banking division of Intesa Sanpaolo, one of Italy’s major banks. Although more than half of the misappropriated funds have since been recovered, approximately €36 million remains missing.
The criminals managed to contact the director of Fideuram using a fake identity on WhatsApp. The message—purportedly from the head of Intesa Sanpaolo—requested assistance with an overseas transfer. Shortly thereafter, a phone call followed in which a deepfake voice, posing as a senior figure at a prominent law firm, confirmed the transaction. The Fideuram director then initiated the transfers to destinations including China and Hong Kong.
In cooperation with authorities in countries such as China, Portugal, and Italy, a portion of the money was subsequently recovered. However, a substantial portion still remains missing.
@anp | NEWS BRAINPORT

report.summary: Scammers used AI deepfake voice and fake WhatsApp identity to steal €95M from Intesa Sanpaolo's Fideuram unit, with €36M still missing.
report.background: AI-powered fraud is escalating as generative voice tools become cheap and accessible. Criminals no longer need technical expertise; they can clone a voice from seconds of audio and combine it with WhatsApp spoofing to impersonate executives. Intesa Sanpaolo, Italy's largest bank, and its Fideuram private banking arm are high-value targets because they handle large transfers. The scam exploited trust in hierarchy and urgency: a fake WhatsApp message from the bank's head, followed by a deepfake call from a purported law firm leader, convinced a director to approve overseas transfers. This mirrors a broader rise in business email compromise and deepfake CEO fraud. While banks have invested in cybersecurity, human verification and cross-border transfer controls remain weak points. Regulators are increasingly focused on operational resilience and AI-related risks.
key_points: The scammers contacted Fideuram's director on WhatsApp, posing as Intesa Sanpaolo's head, and requested help with an overseas transfer. A follow-up call used a deepfake voice impersonating a senior lawyer to confirm the request. The director then authorized transfers to China and Hong Kong.

Approximately €95 million was misappropriated. More than half was recovered through cooperation with authorities in China, Portugal, and Italy, but roughly €36 million remains missing. The scale makes it one of the largest known AI-assisted bank frauds.

Generative AI voice cloning tools are now inexpensive and widely available. A short audio sample can produce a convincing deepfake. Combined with messaging app impersonation, this creates a potent social engineering attack that bypasses traditional email phishing filters.

Recovering funds required international cooperation. The transfers to China and Hong Kong complicated tracing. While some money was frozen, jurisdictional delays and rapid transfers can leave significant losses unrecovered. This highlights the need for faster cross-border financial crime response.

Despite advanced cybersecurity, the attack succeeded by manipulating a trusted employee. Urgency and authority cues overwhelmed verification protocols. It shows that technical defenses must be paired with strict callback procedures and employee training, especially for high-value transfers.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this incident intensifies pressure to build provenance, watermarking, and detection into voice models. Developers must consider misuse safeguards, consent for voice cloning, and API monitoring. Banks and enterprises will likely accelerate investment in deepfake detection, liveness verification, and multi-factor approval for transfers. Regular users face growing risk of voice scams from family emergency calls to fake bank requests; they should verify unexpected requests through a separate channel. Regulators may tighten rules under DORA and the EU AI Act, treating deepfake fraud as a critical operational risk. Overall, trust in voice and video communication is eroding, and identity verification will shift toward cryptographic and behavioral signals.
report.tools: Detection and defense tools to watch: Pindrop, Reality Defender, Resemble Detect, and Hive AI for deepfake audio/video detection. Open-source options include ASVspoof and DeepFake-o-meter for audio deepfake detection, and FaceForensics++ datasets for research. Enterprises should also explore FIDO2 phishing-resistant authentication, call-back verification platforms, and transaction monitoring systems like Featurespace or Feedzai.
